lessonTitle: The LMTD Method for Heat Exchangers

blocks.text: A refinery oil cooler works perfectly on the day it is commissioned, but a year later the oil leaves 15 K too hot. Nothing has broken: a thin film of scale on the tube walls has added thermal resistance and cut the overall heat transfer coefficient. Engineers allow for that in the design with a fouling resistance.

blocks.markdown: A heat exchanger transfers heat between two fluids separated by a wall. The heat flow is written $q=UA\Delta T_m$, where $A$ is the heat transfer area (m$^2$), $\Delta T_m$ is a mean temperature difference between the fluids and $U$ is the **overall heat transfer coefficient** (W/m$^2$K). The difficulty is that the temperature difference between the fluids changes along the exchanger, so we need the right average.

blocks.title: Overall coefficient U
blocks.text: $U$ is the reciprocal of the total thermal resistance per unit area between the two fluid streams. For a plane or thin wall of thickness $t$ and conductivity $k$: $1/U=1/h_i+R''_{f,i}+t/k+R''_{f,o}+1/h_o$, where $R''_f$ is a fouling resistance per unit area (m$^2$K/W) accounting for deposits. For a tube, $U$ must say whether it is referred to the inner or outer area.

blocks.title: Overall coefficient with fouling
blocks.prompt: A shell-and-tube oil cooler has water inside thin steel tubes ($h_i=2500$ W/m$^2$K, fouling $R''_{f,i}=0.0002$ m$^2$K/W) and hot oil outside ($h_o=350$ W/m$^2$K, fouling $R''_{f,o}=0.0004$ m$^2$K/W). The wall is 2 mm of steel with $k=45$ W/m K (typical). Treating the wall as plane (the tube is thin so inner and outer areas are nearly equal), find the overall coefficient with and without fouling.

steps.text: The heat passes in series through five resistances per unit area: inside film, inside fouling, wall, outside fouling, outside film. Series resistances per unit area add.
Clean (no fouling): $1/U_c=0.00330$, so $U_c=302.9$ W/m$^2$K. Fouling reduces $U$ by 15%.

blocks.answer: $U\approx256$ W/m$^2$K fouled versus 303 clean. The oil-side film dominates the resistance (since $h_o$ is smallest) and the fouling adds a further 15% of the total.

blocks.markdown: Along a heat exchanger the local temperature difference $\Delta T=T_h-T_c$ varies. Applying the energy balance to a differential element, $dq=U\,dA\,(T_h-T_c)$, and integrating with constant $U$ and constant specific heats gives the **log-mean temperature difference** (LMTD). The two end differences $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ depend on the flow arrangement.

blocks.latex: q=UA\,\Delta T_{lm},\qquad \Delta T_{lm}=\frac{\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)}
blocks.caption: LMTD for a single-pass exchanger with constant U and c_p, no losses to surroundings

rows: Fluids enter at opposite ends; $T_{c,o}$ may exceed $T_{h,o}$
Fluids enter at the same end; $T_{c,o}$ cannot exceed $T_{h,o}$
blocks.caption: End temperature differences for the LMTD (subscripts: h hot, c cold, i inlet, o outlet)

blocks.markdown: Because the log-mean is always less than the arithmetic mean (unless the two differences are equal, when $\Delta T_{lm}=\Delta T_1$), using the plain average would underestimate the required area. For the same four terminal temperatures, counterflow has the larger LMTD and therefore needs the smaller area.

blocks.title: Area of a counterflow oil cooler
blocks.prompt: Oil ($\dot m=1.2$ kg/s, $c_p=2100$ J/kg K, typical) is cooled from 150 $^\circ$C to 90 $^\circ$C by water entering at 25 $^\circ$C and leaving at 55 $^\circ$C. Using the fouled overall coefficient $U=256$ W/m$^2$K from the previous example, find the area needed for counterflow, and compare with parallel flow.

steps.text: Duty from the oil: $q=\dot m c_p(T_{h,i}-T_{h,o})=1.2\times2100\times60=151.2$ kW. (The water capacity rate is then $q/30=5040$ W/K.)
Counterflow end differences: hot inlet faces cold outlet, so $\Delta T_1=T_{h,i}-T_{c,o}=150-55=95$ K and hot outlet faces cold inlet, $\Delta T_2=T_{h,o}-T_{c,i}=90-25=65$ K.
Parallel flow, same terminal temperatures: $\Delta T_1=150-25=125$ K, $\Delta T_2=90-55=35$ K, $\Delta T_{lm}=70.7$ K and $A=8.34$ m$^2$, which is 12% larger.

blocks.answer: Counterflow needs $A\approx7.5$ m$^2$; parallel flow would need about 8.3 m$^2$ because its log-mean difference is only 71 K.

items: Use an energy balance on the stream with known inlet and outlet temperatures: $q=\dot mc_p\Delta T$.
Find the missing outlet temperature from the other stream's energy balance, $q=C_c(T_{c,o}-T_{c,i})$.
Write $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ for the arrangement, then $\Delta T_{lm}$.
Determine $U$ from the film coefficients, wall and fouling resistances.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: Do not mix up the pairings: in counterflow it is hot inlet with cold outlet. If $\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2$ the formula gives $0/0$ and the LMTD equals that common value. Do not add fouling resistances as $h$ values: they are resistances ($R''$) and add to $1/U$. LMTD for a multipass or cross-flow exchanger needs a correction factor (not covered here).

blocks.title: Fouling margin
blocks.text: The clean $U$ is optimistic. A design must use the fouled $U$, so the exchanger is oversized (more area) to keep its duty after deposits build up.

points: Counterflow: $\Delta T_1=T_{h,i}-T_{c,o}$ and $\Delta T_2=T_{h,o}-T_{c,i}$. Parallel: $\Delta T_1=T_{h,i}-T_{c,i}$ and $\Delta T_2=T_{h,o}-T_{c,o}$.
$\Delta T_{lm}=(\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2)/\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)$; counterflow gives the larger value and smaller area.
Required area $A=q/(U\Delta T_{lm})$; fouling raises the area needed.

questions.stem: In a counterflow heat exchanger, the temperature differences used in the LMTD are

distractorRationale.b: These are the end differences for parallel flow.
distractorRationale.c: These are temperature changes of each stream, not the difference between the streams at an end.
distractorRationale.d: These pair the wrong ends of the exchanger for counterflow.

questions.explanation: In counterflow the hot fluid enters at the end where the cold fluid leaves, so that end has $T_{h,i}-T_{c,o}$; the other end has $T_{h,o}-T_{c,i}$. The pairs are always differences between the two streams at the same end of the exchanger.

questions.stem: When fouling builds up on the tube surfaces of an exchanger, with the film coefficients unchanged, the overall coefficient $U$

options.text: increases, because the deposit is a good conductor
is unchanged, because it depends only on the film coefficients
increases, because the surface becomes rougher
decreases, because fouling adds a thermal resistance in series

questions.correctOptionText: decreases, because fouling adds a thermal resistance in series

distractorRationale.a: Deposits are usually poor conductors, and in any case they add a resistance.
distractorRationale.b: $U$ includes every series resistance, including fouling.
distractorRationale.c: Roughness may change $h$, but fouling resistance itself lowers $U$.

questions.explanation: Fouling resistances $R''_f$ add to $1/U$, so $U$ falls and the exchanger delivers less duty for the same area and temperatures. Designers therefore apply a fouling allowance.

questions.stem: In a parallel-flow exchanger, hot fluid cools from 120 $^\circ$C to 70 $^\circ$C while cold fluid heats from 20 $^\circ$C to 60 $^\circ$C. Find the log-mean temperature difference in K.
questions.explanation: For parallel flow, $\Delta T_1=120-20=100$ K at the inlet end and $\Delta T_2=70-60=10$ K at the outlet end. So $\Delta T_{lm}=(100-10)/\ln(100/10)=39.09$ K. The cold outlet (60 $^\circ$C) is below the hot outlet (70 $^\circ$C), as it must be in parallel flow.

questions.stem: Hot exhaust gas cools from 400 $^\circ$C to 250 $^\circ$C in a counterflow heat exchanger while water is heated from 30 $^\circ$C to 90 $^\circ$C. Find the log-mean temperature difference in K.
questions.explanation: Counterflow: $\Delta T_1=T_{h,i}-T_{c,o}=400-90=310$ K and $\Delta T_2=T_{h,o}-T_{c,i}=250-30=220$ K. $\Delta T_{lm}=(310-220)/\ln(310/220)=262.4$ K, slightly below the arithmetic mean of 265 K.

questions.stem: A thin-walled tube (wall resistance negligible) has an inside film coefficient of 1500 W/m$^2$K and an outside film coefficient of 800 W/m$^2$K. The fouling resistances are $R''_{f,i}=0.0003$ m$^2$K/W and $R''_{f,o}=0.0001$ m$^2$K/W. Find the overall coefficient $U$ in W/m$^2$K, treating inner and outer areas as equal.
For the same terminal temperatures and the same $U$, which statement about LMTD and area is correct?

options.text: Parallel flow has the larger LMTD and so needs a smaller area
Both arrangements have the same LMTD for the same terminal temperatures
Counterflow has the larger LMTD and so needs a smaller area than parallel flow
The area is independent of LMTD since $q$ is fixed

questions.correctOptionText: Counterflow has the larger LMTD and so needs a smaller area than parallel flow

distractorRationale.a: It is the reverse: parallel flow has a small end difference at the outlet.
distractorRationale.b: The end differences are paired differently, so the LMTDs differ.

questions.explanation: Counterflow keeps a more even temperature difference along the exchanger, so its log-mean is larger. Since $A=q/(U\Delta T_{lm})$, a larger $\Delta T_{lm}$ means a smaller area.

questions.stem: If the two end temperature differences of an exchanger are equal, $\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2$, the LMTD formula is indeterminate ($0/0$) but the LMTD equals that common difference.
questions.explanation: As $\Delta T_1\to\Delta T_2$, the limit of $(\Delta T_1-\Delta T_2)/\ln(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2)$ is $\Delta T_1$ by L'Hopital's rule. This happens for a balanced counterflow exchanger with equal capacity rates, where the temperature difference is uniform along the length.

questions.stem: Define the overall heat transfer coefficient and explain why a fouling resistance is added to $1/U$ instead of being added to $h$. Say which area $U$ must be referred to for a tube.
markingGuide: $U$ is the reciprocal of the sum of thermal resistances per unit area between the two fluids: $q=UA\Delta T$.
Series resistances add; fouling is a layer in series with each film and the wall, so $R''_f$ adds to $1/U$ (it is not a convective coefficient).
A large fouling resistance lowers $U$, so more area is needed for the same duty.
For a tube $U$ must state the reference area (inner or outer), because $U_iA_i=U_oA_o$ for the same total resistance.
questions.explanation: The answer rests on the series-resistance picture. The reference-area point stops students from mixing inner and outer areas for tube exchangers.

questions.stem: Explain why, for the same inlet and outlet temperatures, a counterflow exchanger needs less surface area than a parallel flow exchanger. State one limitation of parallel flow on outlet temperatures.
markingGuide: For fixed terminal temperatures the duty $q$ is fixed, and $A=q/(U\Delta T_{lm})$.
In counterflow the end differences ($T_{h,i}-T_{c,o}$ and $T_{h,o}-T_{c,i}$) are more equal, giving a larger LMTD than parallel flow, whose outlet difference $T_{h,o}-T_{c,o}$ is small.
A larger LMTD gives a smaller $A$.
In parallel flow the cold outlet cannot exceed the hot outlet temperature, whereas counterflow allows it.
questions.explanation: The log-mean average is larger when the two end differences are closer. Parallel flow forces the streams to approach each other at the outlet, wasting driving force.

questions.stem: A counterflow exchanger heats 0.8 kg/s of water ($c_p=4180$ J/kg K) from 15 $^\circ$C to 45 $^\circ$C using hot water entering at 85 $^\circ$C and leaving at 50 $^\circ$C. The inside film coefficient is 3000 W/m$^2$K, the outside is 1500 W/m$^2$K, the stainless wall is 1.5 mm thick with $k=16$ W/m K and the total fouling resistance is 0.0003 m$^2$K/W (plane-wall approximation, equal areas). Find the required heat transfer area in m$^2$.
questions.explanation: The duty is $q=0.8\times4180\times30=100320$ W. Resistances: $1/3000+1/1500+0.0015/16+0.0003=0.001394$, so $U=717.5$ W/m$^2$K. Counterflow differences are $85-45=40$ K and $50-15=35$ K, giving $\Delta T_{lm}=37.44$ K. Then $A=q/(U\Delta T_{lm})=100320/(717.5\times37.44)=3.73$ m$^2$.
